language: science

  readySelector: "#gpanel"

explainClip:
  query: { code: "@boards.yml#explain", fresh: 1, id: explain }
  caption: "Newton's first law"
  say: "Moving things need no force to keep going, only to change their motion."
  clip:
    - caption: { text: "No push. Friction is the only force, so the puck slows down.", say: "With no push, friction is the only force, so the puck slows down." }
    - click: "Play"
    - wait: 3200
    - click: "Friction: on"
    - click: "Reset"
    - caption: { text: "Friction off: no forces at all.", say: "Now switch friction off, so there are no forces at all." }
    - click: "Play"
    - wait: 2500
    - expect: { selector: "body", contains: "speed 3 m/s" }
    - caption: { text: "It keeps going at the same speed: no net force, no change.", say: "It keeps going at the same speed: no net force, no change." }
    - wait: 600

For two thousand years people agreed with Aristotle that a moving thing needs a force to keep it going, and you're about to put that idea to the test.

## Engage: the sliding puck

```step
stage: predict
insight: "The Aristotelian answers (the force stays in the puck; it needs a push to keep going) are the target; committing first makes the coasting puck surprising."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A hockey stick hits a puck, then stops touching it. The puck slides across perfectly smooth ice (no friction). What do you predict happens?"
  options: ["It slows down as the force of the hit runs out", "It keeps sliding at the same speed", "It stops straight away", "It speeds up"]
  actual: "It keeps sliding at the same speed. With no net force, nothing changes its motion. The 'force of the hit' isn't stored inside it: the force only acted while the stick touched it."
```

## Explore: push, then let go

```step
stage: run
insight: "Removing every force from a moving object and watching it coast confronts the 'motion needs force' belief directly."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#puck", height: 640 }
check: { type: board, text: "Get the puck moving, then turn the push to 0 and friction off, and watch it coast for a few seconds.", when: "t >= 3 and P = 0 and F = 0 and v > 0" }
hint: ["The puck has to still be moving once both the push and friction are gone, so think about which one to change first.", "The line under the board shows the time, the speed and the acceleration, and the Friction button says whether it's on or off."]
```

Press **Play** to push the puck. After a second or two, slide **Push** to 0 and turn **Friction** off. Watch the graph and the dots.

## Explain: the first law

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Stating the law, then using it to explain the coasting puck and the everyday slowing down, replaces the Aristotelian model instead of adding to it."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "With no push and no friction, what did the puck do?"
      options: ["Kept moving at a constant speed", "Slowed down gradually", "Stopped"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Check the graph: a flat line means constant speed.", "Check the dots: they stayed evenly spaced."]
      explain: "No net force, no change in motion: Newton's first law."
    hint: ["Think back to the board, and look at what the speed–time graph did once the push and friction were both gone.", "The dots under the track are dropped every half second, so their spacing shows whether the puck was covering the same distance each time."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Which statement is Newton's first law?"
      options: ["An object stays at rest or keeps moving at a constant velocity unless a net force acts on it", "A moving object needs a force to keep it moving", "Every object eventually comes to rest", "Heavier objects are harder to keep moving"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That is Aristotle's idea, which the puck contradicts.", "It stops only when a force, often friction, acts against it.", "Mass makes it harder to change motion, not to keep it going."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "So why does a ball rolling on grass slow down and stop?"
      options: ["Friction and air resistance act against it: a net force backwards", "Its force runs out", "Gravity pulls it backwards", "Balls naturally stop"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "There is no store of force inside the ball.", "Gravity pulls down, not backwards, on flat ground.", "Only because a force acts: on smooth ice it goes much further."]
      explain: "The 'hidden' forces, friction and air resistance, are the net force that slows it."
    hint: "Something has to change the ball's motion, so what's touching it while it rolls along?"
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "What is inertia?"
      options: ["An object's tendency to resist changes in its motion (more mass, more inertia)", "A force that keeps objects moving", "The friction on a moving object"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Inertia isn't a force: it is resistance to a change in motion.", "Friction is a force; inertia is a property of the object."]
    hint: "Think about the puck coasting on the board with the push at 0 and friction off, and ask whether anything was pushing it along."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I explained why a moving object doesn't need a force to keep moving, and what really slows things down." }
```

## Elaborate: friction is the hidden force

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "Running the same puck with friction on shows the everyday slowing as a net force effect, completing the replacement of the Aristotelian model."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#friction", height: 640 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Let the moving puck slide with no push (friction on) until it stops.", when: "t >= 1 and v = 0" }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Friction is 2 N and the puck's mass is 1 kg. While it slides, what is happening?"
      options: ["A net force of 2 N backwards makes it slow down steadily", "Its push slowly runs out", "Friction is balanced by its motion"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "There is no push at all, so the push is 0 N.", "Motion isn't a force; nothing balances friction here."]
      explain: "The only horizontal force is friction, so it is the net force. The graph slopes down in a straight line: steady slowing."
```

## Elaborate: seatbelts

```step
stage: modify
tier: wider
insight: "The unrestrained passenger is the first law in a high-stakes setting: the car is stopped by a force; the passenger isn't."
check:
  type: question
  q: "A car hits a barrier and stops suddenly. A passenger isn't wearing a seatbelt. Using the first law, what happens to them?"
  options: ["They keep moving forward at the car's old speed until something (the dashboard, windscreen) exerts a force on them", "They are thrown forward by a force from the crash", "They stop with the car"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "No force throws them forward: they simply keep going while the car stops.", "Only if a force acts on them: the seatbelt provides it, gently, over a longer time."]
  explain: "A seatbelt applies the force that stops the passenger along with the car, spread over a little more time and a wide area."
```

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I compared my prediction about the puck with what the board showed." }
```

Write one sentence: "At first I thought… Now I think… because…"

**Revision summary**

- **Newton's first law:** an object stays at rest, or keeps moving at a constant velocity, unless a **net force** acts on it.
- A moving object does **not** need a force to keep moving. A force is needed to **change** motion.
- Everyday objects slow down because of **friction and air resistance**: hidden forces that are the net force.
- **Inertia** is an object's resistance to changes in its motion; more mass, more inertia.

```teacher
summary: Students state Newton's first law and explain why a moving object with
  no net force continues at constant velocity, confronting the Aristotelian idea
  that motion needs a continuous force (AC9S10U05, node 2, a hinge node).
time: 25
timing: Engage and Explore 8 min · Explain 9 min · Evaluate 3 min · Typical adds
  4 min, Wider about 3 min
goals:
  - I can state Newton's first law.
  - I can explain why a moving object with no net force keeps a constant
    velocity.
  - I can identify friction as the hidden force that slows everyday objects.
before: >
  A concept tutorial for introducing or revising the idea; it does not replace
  air tracks or a puck on a smooth floor. Set the width with `?width=minimum`,
  `typical` (default) or `wider`.


  The Aristotelian view survives exposure to the correct definition unless it is
  confronted. The Explore board is that confrontation: commit to a prediction,
  then watch the puck coast.


  Board notes: motion is left and right only; friction is a fixed 2 N while
  sliding.
running:
  - "Engage: ask students who chose 'slows down' to say where the force of the
    hit is stored. Keep their answers for Evaluate."
  - "Explore: the check needs push 0 and friction off while moving. If a student
    turns friction off first, the puck speeds up: ask why."
  - "Explain: the 'why does a ball stop' question is where the hidden force gets
    named."
  - "In your own words: the reply to 'the force is still in it' is the evidence."
struggle: Letting go of 'a moving thing needs a push to keep going'. When a
  student says the force ran out, ask what the graph did with push 0 and
  friction off.
stuck:
  - see: A student says the puck slows because the force runs out.
    ask: On the board, with push 0 and friction off, did the graph slope down?
    fix: No, it stayed flat. Nothing was stored; with no net force, nothing changes.
  - see: A student says inertia is a force.
    ask: What pushes the puck along when it coasts?
    fix: Nothing. Inertia is the tendency not to change motion, not a push.
  - see: A student confuses constant velocity with zero force.
    ask: Could there be forces on a car moving at a constant 60 km/h?
    fix: Yes, balanced ones. The net force is zero.
stretch: Voyager 1 is coasting out of the solar system with its engines off.
  Will it ever stop? What could change its motion?
support: "Give the frame: 'There is / isn't a net force, so the motion stays the
  same / changes, because …'."
leads: >
  Next: acceleration as a defined quantity (node 3), then F = ma (node 4).


  In class: a puck or dry-ice block on a smooth bench; a coin on a card flicked
  off a cup (inertia).
exit:
  q: A spacecraft coasts through empty space with its engines off. Describe its
    motion and explain.
  a: "It keeps moving at a constant velocity: there is no net force (no friction
    or air resistance), so by the first law its motion doesn't change."
explain: >
  **Newton's first law:** an object stays at rest or keeps moving at a constant
  velocity unless a **net force** acts on it.


  Moving things don't need a push to keep going; they need a force to change
  their motion. Friction and air resistance are why everyday things slow down.
```
